paragraphs: Once public service is no longer the citizens’ chief business, and they would rather serve with their money than with their persons, the State is close to falling. When war calls them out, they pay troops and stay home. When the council must meet, they appoint deputies and stay home. Through laziness and money, they end up with soldiers to enslave their country and representatives to sell it.

Personal services turn into money payments because of the bustle of commerce and the arts, the greedy self-interest in profit, and softness and love of comforts. Men give up part of their profits so they can have leisure to increase them. Make gifts of money, and you will soon be in chains. The word _finance_ is a slavish word, unknown in the city-state. In a truly free country, the citizens do everything with their own hands and nothing with money. Far from paying to be excused from their duties, they would pay for the privilege of doing them themselves. I am far from sharing the common view: I think forced labor is less opposed to liberty than taxes are.

The better a State’s constitution is, the more public affairs encroach on private ones in the citizens’ minds. Private affairs even matter much less, because the sum of the common happiness supplies a larger part of each person’s happiness, and so there is less left for him to look for in his own concerns. In a well-ordered city, every man rushes to the assemblies. Under a bad government, no one will take a step to attend them. No one is interested in what happens there, it is foreseen that the general will will not prevail, and domestic concerns swallow up everything. Good laws lead to better ones, and bad laws bring worse. Once a man says of the State’s affairs _What does it matter to me?_ the State can be given up for lost.

Cooling patriotism, busy private interest, the vast size of States, conquest and the abuse of government gave rise to the idea of deputies or representatives of the people in the national assemblies. In some countries men have dared to call these deputies the Third Estate. In this arrangement the private interest of two orders comes first and second, and the public interest gets only third place.

Sovereignty cannot be represented, for the same reason that it cannot be given away. It lies essentially in the general will, and a will cannot be represented: it is either itself or something else, with nothing in between. The people’s deputies, therefore, are not and cannot be its representatives. They are only its stewards, and they cannot conclude anything definitively. Any law the people has not ratified in person is null and void — it is not a law at all. The people of England thinks it is free, but it is badly mistaken. It is free only while it elects members of parliament. As soon as they are elected, slavery overtakes it, and it is nothing. The way it uses its brief moments of liberty shows that it deserves to lose them.

The idea of representation is modern. It comes to us from feudal government, that unjust and absurd system that degrades humanity and dishonors the name of man. In ancient republics, and even in monarchies, the people never had representatives, and the word itself was unknown. It is very strange that in Rome, where the tribunes were so sacred, nobody ever imagined they could usurp the functions of the people. Among so great a multitude, they never once tried to pass a plebiscitum on their own authority. Still, we can get an idea of the difficulties a large crowd sometimes caused from what happened in the time of the Gracchi, when some of the citizens had to vote from the rooftops.

Where right and liberty are everything, drawbacks count for nothing. This wise people valued everything at its true worth. It let its lictors do what its tribunes would never have dared attempt, since it never feared that its lictors might try to represent it.

To explain how the tribunes sometimes did represent the people, it is enough to see how the government represents the Sovereign. Law is purely the declaration of the general will, so clearly the people cannot be represented when it exercises the legislative power. The executive power, however, is only the force applied to give the law effect, and there the people can and should be represented. This shows that, looked at closely, very few nations would turn out to have laws. However that may be, the tribunes held no executive power, so they could never represent the Roman people by right of the powers entrusted to them, but only by usurping those of the senate.

In Greece, the people did everything it had to do for itself, and it was constantly gathered in the public square. The Greeks lived in a mild climate and had no natural greed. Slaves did their work, and their great concern was liberty. You do not have these advantages, so how can you keep the same rights? Your harsher climates add to your needs;[1] for half the year your public squares cannot be lived in, and the flat sound of your languages makes them unfit to be heard in the open air. You give up more for profit than for liberty, and you fear poverty more than slavery.

What then? Can liberty be maintained only with the support of slavery? Perhaps so. Extremes meet. Whatever lies outside the course of nature has its drawbacks, and civil society most of all. There are unhappy circumstances in which we can keep our liberty only at the expense of others, and the citizen can be perfectly free only when the slave is most utterly a slave. Sparta was like that. As for you, modern peoples, you have no slaves, but you are slaves yourselves; you pay for their liberty with your own. You can boast of this preference as you like, but I find more cowardice in it than humanity.

None of this means that we must have slaves, or that the right of slavery is legitimate. I am simply explaining why modern peoples, who believe they are free, have representatives, and why ancient peoples had none. In any case, the moment a people lets itself be represented, it is no longer free, and it no longer exists.

Taking everything into account, I do not see how the Sovereign can go on exercising its rights among us, unless the city is very small. But if the city is very small, will it not be conquered? No. Later I will show how a great people’s[2] strength against outsiders can be combined with the convenient organization and good order of a small State.
